claims.text: Tikuli is the local word in Bihar for the bindi, the bright dot that women wear on the forehead between the eyebrows.

quotes.quote: The word 'tikuli' is the local term for 'bindi', which is usually a bright, colorful dot that women wear between their brows.
The word 'tikuli' is the local term for 'bindi', which is usually a bright, colourful dot that women wear between their brows.
Tikuli is the term that is locally used for bindis, which are essentially colorful dots that women wear as accessories between their eyebrows.

claims.text: The name tikuli comes from tikli, a Hindi word that means bindi or dot.

quotes.quote: The name Tikuli comes from the word 'tikli', which means 'bindi' or 'dot' in Hindi.
is derived from the Hindi word 'tikli,' meaning bindi-a traditional decorative ornamentation worn on the forehead by Indian women

claims.text: Modern tikuli painting uses glossy enamel paints on hardboard or medium-density fibreboard in place of the glass of the old ornaments.

quotes.quote: Modern Tikuli practice shifts from glass to hardboard or medium-density fibreboard and uses enamel paints that produce a glossy, durable surface.
Artists typically begin with hardboards and use enamel paints to create complex compositions.

claims.text: Tikuli designs today decorate wall paintings, wall plates, coasters, table mats, trays, pen stands, earrings, fabrics and saris instead of forehead bindis.

quotes.quote: Today, instead of tikulis that were used as bindis, the art form adorns wall paintings, coasters, table mats, trays, pen-stands, earrings, as on fabrics and saris.
to make decorative wall plates, coasters, table mats, wall hanging, trays, pen stands and other utility items

claims.text: Tikuli art has become a source of income and empowerment for women artisans in Bihar.

quotes.quote: However, in today's time, Tikuli art serves as a source of empowerment for the women of Bihar.
One such art form from Bihar is Tikuli art, empowering the state's women artisans.
Women artisans in particular use Tikuli work as a source of income and as a way to claim visibility within local craft economies.

claims.text: Present-day tikuli painting shows a clear influence of Mithila or Madhubani painting in its composition and themes.

quotes.quote: Mithila painting has a clear influence in the paintings of Tikuli art at present.
Influenced by Madhubani in terms of composition and themes
Tikuli has a shadow of the famous Madhubani art techniques.
Tikuli Art bears a resemblance to Madhubani painting, with Mithila's style clearly influencing contemporary Tikuli works.

claims.text: Tikuli art combines the traditions of Madhubani art and Patna Kalam art with a Japanese technique of enamel paint on timber.

quotes.quote: the art form that combines the traditions of Madhubani art, Patna Kalam art and a Japanese art technique of using enamel paints on timber

claims.text: Mithila painting is done on paper and cloth, whereas tikuli painting is done on hardboard or MDF.

quotes.quote: while Mithila painting is done on paper and cloth, painting in Tikuli painting is done on hardboard MDF
Mithila paintings typically adorn paper and fabric, whereas Tikuli paintings are crafted on hardboard or MDF.

claims.text: Tikuli paintings are relatively small, while Mithila paintings are usually larger.

quotes.quote: In Mithila painting the paintings are larger while in Tikuli painting are relatively small.
Mithila paintings tend to be larger in scale, whereas Tikuli paintings are generally more compact.

claims.text: Tikuli painting depicts the life of common people alongside religion, while Mithila painting has kept mainly to religious subjects.

quotes.quote: Mithila painting has been confined mainly by the painters to religious subjects, while the Tikuli style depicts the life of the common people along with religion.
Mithila paintings often explore religious themes, while Tikuli art depicts everyday life alongside spiritual motifs.

claims.text: Common tikuli themes are festivals of Bihar, Indian wedding scenes and Krishna Leela, with many stories of Lord Krishna.

quotes.quote: The themes mostly revolve around festivals of Bihar, Indian wedding scenes, and Krishna Leela.
featuring vibrant scenes of Indian weddings, traditional festivals like Chhath Puja, Diwali, and Holi, as well as epic tales from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Krishna Leela
The theme of the paintings are usually drawn from Indian folklore, especially from the stories of Lord Krishna.

claims.text: Tikuli enamel colours are mostly bright crimson, yellow, cobalt blue and deep green, chosen to stand out against a dark base.

quotes.quote: The enamel paints used in the craft are mostly bright crimson, yellow, cobalt blue and deep green, so that the designs come out vibrantly over a dark fibreboard.

claims.text: In the revived craft, women painted the designs in single strokes, in a complementary colour scheme built from primary colours.

quotes.quote: was painted by women in single strokes in a complimentary colour scheme using primary colors to create a piece of art

claims.text: A Bihar Museum record describes a tikuli painting by Ashok Kumar Biswas that shows the whole life of Krishna, from his birth to his final departure.

quotes.quote: This Tikuli painting by Padma Shri awardee Ashok Kumar Biswas beautifully captures the entirety of Krishna's life. The artwork illustrates key moments from his birth to his final departure

claims.text: Tikuli art is believed to have originated in Patna about 800 years ago.

quotes.quote: It is believed that this art originated approximately 800 years ago in the region around Patna.
Originating in the city of Patna, the skill is thought to date back approximately 800 years.
Tikuli art originated 800 years ago from Patna.
Tikuli is a type of hand painting and its history spread over 800 years. The painting with its modern evolution and varied manifestations, find its origin in Patna, Bihar.
Tikuli art originated in Patna over 800 years ago.

claims.text: Tikuli art is an ancient craft that dates back to the Mauryan period, when royal and aristocratic women wore tikulis.

quotes.quote: reviving Tikuli Art, an ancient craft dating back to the Mauryan period
Historically, Tikuli art was practiced during the Mauryan period, as evidenced by ancient sculptures depicting women with ornate bindis.
There is archeological evidence that the tikulis were a part and parcel of the ornaments used by women in the Mauryan era, particularly royalty and aristocratic women
It started as a way for bindi-making artists to earn more income and has roots going back to the Mauryan period.

claims.text: Tikuli art originated in Bihar and has its roots in the Mithila region.

quotes.quote: Tikuli art is a traditional folk art form that originated in Bihar and has its roots in the Mithila region.

claims.text: The Mughals patronised tikuli art, and the craft flourished under Mughal rule.

quotes.quote: The Mughals also patronized this form of art and greatly appreciated its importance.
It was not only patronized by the royals but it flourished during the Mughal rule.
This art form received patronage and encouragement during the Mughal period.
The Mughals were active patrons of the art form, and appreciated its many salient features.

claims.text: Traders from distant states of northern and western India came to Patna to buy embellished tikulis in bulk.

quotes.quote: Traders from the far-off states of northern and western India to Patna where bulk purchasers of the gorgeously embellished Tikulis
the tikuli art-form managed to influence traders from across the country to flock to Patna to buy Tikuli art in bulk

claims.text: Tikulis were once produced in Patna on a mass scale and exported to cities such as Kanpur and Delhi.

quotes.quote: The art of making bindis commercially in such an elaborate manner flourished in the city of Patna. The tikulis used to be produced in a mass scale and were exported to cities like Kanpur and Delhi

claims.text: In the past, tikulis were worn mainly by queens and aristocratic women, who prized them as possessions.

quotes.quote: In the past times, Tikuli were mainly used by queens and aristocrat women. Beautiful hand crafted Tikuli were revered as proud possessions of the women.
Tikuli were mainly adorned by Queens and Aristocrat women of yore.

claims.text: Around the 17th century, craftsmen began making miniature art pieces with the tikuli method, motifs and thick, shiny paint.

quotes.quote: Then around the 17th century craftsmen started making miniature art pieces in the same method, with the same tikuli motifs and thick, shiny paint.

claims.text: Old tikulis began as glass melted in a furnace and blown like a balloon into a thin sheet.

quotes.quote: Earlier, the glass was melted in the furnace as a balloon.
Originally, it involved melting glass, blowing it into a thin sheet
Initially, glass was melted in a furnace and shaped like a balloon.

claims.text: Once the glass had cooled, it was cut into round pieces of various sizes with a special tool.

quotes.quote: When cooled, it was harvested to the required size with a special tool.
The glass sheet was cut into round pieces in different sizes
Glass was melted in a furnace and then cut into the desired shape.

claims.text: The cut glass pieces were then overlaid with gold foil, or with gold or silver foil in one account.

quotes.quote: Then gold work was pasted on it.
Subsequently, it was overlaid with gold or silver foil.
It entailed melting glass, tracing a pattern in natural colors, and then decorating it with gold foil

claims.text: Designs of flowers, leaves, gods and goddesses were then scratched in with a sharp bamboo point and filled with colours.

quotes.quote: After that, with the sharp pencil of the boss, pictures of flowers, leaves, gods and goddesses were scratched and painted with various colors.
with sharp bamboo tools, traced patterns on the tikulis and filled them with natural colours
Thereafter, images of deities, nature-related motifs and other designs were etched onto it.

claims.text: Finally, the tikuli received a coat of adhesive, given as acacia glue or gond, and was rubbed with a soft cloth.

quotes.quote: Then it was coated with acacia glue. In the end, she was rubbed with a soft cloth.
the final touch was a layer of gond (adhesive) applied to the tikuli before it was ready to be used

claims.text: Making a single glass tikuli took seven to ten days.

quotes.quote: Due to this process it took seven to ten days to make one piece of Tikuli.
The creation of a single Tikuli would take approximately seven to ten days.
crafting a single piece of Tikuli could take anywhere from seven to ten days

claims.text: Three artisans shared the making of a tikuli: one blew and cut the glass, one applied the gold, and one scratched and coloured the design.

quotes.quote: One artist inflated the glass as a balloon and cut it with a special kind of scissors, another made gold work on it, and the third scratched it with a bamboo pointed pencil and filled them with different colors.
One artisan would shape and cut the glass, another would apply intricate goldwork, and a third would etch designs with a precision tool and fill them with vibrant hues.

claims.text: Muslim artisans cut the glass sheets into round pieces and handed them to Hindu artists, who covered them with gold foil.

quotes.quote: The glass sheet was cut into round pieces in different sizes, a work undertaken by Muslim artisans, and then handed over to Hindu artists who covered the tikulis with gold foil.

claims.text: The painter and designer Upendra Maharathi began reviving tikuli art in 1954.

lede.text: Tikuli is the local word in Bihar for the bindi, and tikuli painting is now made with glossy enamel paints on hardboard or MDF board.
It is believed to have originated in Patna about 800 years ago, while other sources trace the craft back to the Mauryan period.
After machine-made bindis replaced the old glass tikulis, Upendra Maharathi began a revival that Ashok Kumar Biswas carried on, turning tikuli into a folk painting.
Today the craft gives livelihood support to about 300-500 artisan families in the Digha, Danapur and Gai Ghat mahallas of Patna town, and is a source of income for women artisans in Bihar.

sentences.text: Tikulis were forehead ornaments worn mainly by queens and aristocratic women, and the Mughals patronised the craft.
Glass was melted and blown into a thin sheet, cut into rounds, covered with gold foil, scratched with designs and coloured, and one tikuli took seven to ten days.
Muslim artisans cut the glass and Hindu artists applied the gold foil, with three artisans sharing each piece.
Under British rule, machine-made bindis replaced tikulis, and the art faced extinction by 1900, or in the mid-20th century by another account.
Upendra Maharathi began reviving the craft in 1954, or in 1950 by one account, after seeing commercial hardboard paintings in Japan.
At the 1982 Asian Games, tikuli paintings were the official gift for all the participating athletes.
Ashok Kumar Biswas carried on the revival after Maharathi died in 1981, and with Shibani Biswas he has kept the art alive since 1974.
Biswas received the Padma Shri in 2024 for reviving tikuli art over five decades.
Tikuli artists first cut hardboard or MDF into round, rectangular, triangular or square pieces.
The board is given 4-5 coats of enamel, or 5-6 in the Danapur cluster, with sanding after each coat until the black or dark brown base is smooth and shiny.
The design outline is traced on tracing paper, dusted with talcum powder and traced onto the base with a pen.
The design is outlined, five colours are filled in one at a time with drying between each, and a black outline is added.
The outline is then finished in white paint, dust is wiped off, and wall hangings get loops or frames.
Another account says the designs are painted in natural pigments mixed with water and gum arabic, then protected with a layer of lacquer.
MDF board and colours are the basic raw materials, with ply board used for coaster stands, trays, mobile stands and boxes.
Enamel paint, bought through a wholesaler in Patna, serves for both the base coat and the ornamentation, and thinner dilutes it.
Enamel makes the surface heatproof and waterproof, which suits coasters, trays and mobile stands.
Round brushes of sizes 0, 00 and 000 are used for painting and flat brushes up to number 30 for the base coat.
The fine brushes are made of squirrel or sable hair.
Because glass was impractical to transport and gold was costly, artists moved to wood and later to hardboard or MDF.
Present-day tikuli painting shows a clear influence of Mithila or Madhubani painting in its composition and themes.
Mithila painting is done on paper and cloth and is usually larger, whereas tikuli painting is done on hardboard or MDF and is relatively small.
Common themes are festivals of Bihar, Indian wedding scenes and Krishna Leela.
The enamel colours are mostly bright crimson, yellow, cobalt blue and deep green against a dark base.
The Asiad gift pictures of 1982 were painted in the style of Jagdamba Devi, and her style came to be accepted as the authentic style of tikuli art.
Traders once came to Patna to buy tikulis in bulk, and tikulis were exported to cities such as Kanpur and Delhi.
According to Ashok Kumar Biswas, Patna, Varanasi and Kolkata are the main hubs for buying and selling tikuli art.
Ashok Kumar Biswas says about 98% of the 7,000-odd tikuli artisans are women, and the Upendra Maharathi institute's director says there were only 300 artisans about a decade earlier.
Until 1984 the government bought tikuli artwork directly from the artists, and a 2017 handicrafts policy trained new artists.
Middlemen acting as agents take a major chunk of the income of tikuli artisans.
In the Danapur cluster workshop survey, a tray was priced at Rs 800 and wall hangings or table mats at Rs 1000 to 2400.
Geographical Indication application 657 for Tikuli Art was withdrawn, and application 1633 was filed in 2025.
